title: SI base quantities and prefixes
prior_knowledge_summary: Every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit.
Reasonable estimates can be built from familiar benchmarks and scale comparisons.
An approximate value should retain an appropriate unit, and impossible scales or false precision should be rejected.
new_learning: The five SI base quantities required here are mass, length, time, electric current and temperature, with base units kilogram, metre, second, ampere and kelvin.
The prefixes pico, nano, micro, milli, centi, deci, kilo, mega, giga and tera represent fixed decimal powers of ten.
A prefixed measurement can be converted by replacing the prefix with its power-of-ten multiplier while keeping the physical quantity unchanged.
not_yet_taught: Applications belonging to later Physics topics

visual_planning.reason: Seven distinct visuals establish the opening timing puzzle, organise the five required base quantity-unit pairs, map the prefix scale, model two conversion directions, expose case sensitivity, explain the kilogram exception and synthesise a reliable conversion route.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Did the two timers record different pulses?
content: One timer displays 0.004 s. Another displays 4 ms. A student says the second pulse lasted much longer because 4 is greater than 0.004. Is that conclusion safe?
The numerical magnitudes look different because the unit scales are different. Before comparing them, we need a shared system of units and a reliable way to read prefixes.

figure.purpose: Create a contradiction that makes a shared unit scale and prefix conversion necessary
figure.brief: Draw two simple digital timer cards on white paper. One reads 0.004 s and the other reads 4 ms. Place a large comparison question mark between them and a small note saying compare the unit scales first. Do not state whether they are equal.
figure.alt_text: Two timer displays show 0.004 seconds and 4 milliseconds, with a question asking how their durations compare.

blocks.title: Start with five shared measurement foundations
content: Scientists need agreed reference units so that a measurement means the same thing in every laboratory. The SI system provides base quantities and one base unit for each.
For this syllabus outcome, learn these five pairs exactly: mass in kilogram (kg), length in metre (m), time in second (s), electric current in ampere (A), and temperature in kelvin (K).

Keep quantity and unit separate. Electric current is a quantity, while ampere is its unit. Temperature is a quantity, while kelvin is its unit. Symbols are case-sensitive: A and K are capital letters, while kg, m and s use lower-case letters.

figure.purpose: Organise the five required base quantities, unit names and symbols without mixing categories
figure.brief: Create a hand-drawn five-row classroom reference card with three columns labelled quantity, base unit and symbol. Rows are mass, length, time, electric current and temperature paired with kilogram kg, metre m, second s, ampere A and kelvin K. Use one small colour accent per column and generous spacing.
figure.alt_text: A five-row reference card pairs mass with kilogram, length with metre, time with second, current with ampere and temperature with kelvin.

blocks.title: A prefix changes the size of the unit
content: A prefix placed before a unit symbol represents a fixed decimal multiplier. It lets us replace a long string of zeroes with a compact scale label.

The required submultiples are pico (p) = 10^-12, nano (n) = 10^-9, micro (μ) = 10^-6, milli (m) = 10^-3, centi (c) = 10^-2 and deci (d) = 10^-1. The required multiples are kilo (k) = 10^3, mega (M) = 10^6, giga (G) = 10^9 and tera (T) = 10^12.
For example, 1 ms means 1 x 10^-3 s, while 1 km means 1 x 10^3 m. The prefix changes the unit scale, not the physical quantity being measured.

figure.purpose: Make the order, symbols and powers of ten of all required prefixes visible as one scale
figure.brief: Draw a horizontal hand-sketched power-of-ten ladder from 10^-12 to 10^12. Mark only p, n, μ, m, c, d, the unprefixed unit at 10^0, then k, M, G and T. Label each mark with its prefix name. Use cool colours for submultiples and warm colours for multiples.
figure.alt_text: A prefix scale orders pico through tera by their powers of ten around an unprefixed unit at ten to the zero.

blocks.title: Replace the prefix with its multiplier
content: Suppose a short pulse lasts 6.5 μs. The prefix micro means 10^-6, so write 6.5 μs = 6.5 x 10^-6 s.
The number becomes small because seconds are a larger unit than microseconds. Keep s attached throughout the conversion so the result remains a complete physical quantity.
Independent check: one microsecond is one millionth of a second. A few microseconds must therefore be far below 1 s, and 6.5 x 10^-6 s has the expected scale.

figure.purpose: Show a complete prefixed-to-unprefixed conversion with the unit carried at every step
figure.brief: Create an annotated three-step notebook layout: 6.5 μs, replace μ by 10^-6, then 6.5 x 10^-6 s. Circle the unchanged physical duration and underline the unit s at each stage. Use arrows and no calculator styling.
figure.alt_text: A three-step conversion replaces micro with ten to the minus six and gives 6.5 times ten to the minus six seconds.

blocks.title: Work backwards to choose a useful prefix
content: Now take a length of 0.0000042 m. Scientific notation gives 4.2 x 10^-6 m. Since 10^-6 is micro, the same length is 4.2 μm.
This is the reverse route: first expose the power of ten, then replace that power with its prefix symbol. The value and unit scale change together, so the physical length stays the same.
Check by expanding the prefix again: 4.2 μm = 4.2 x 10^-6 m = 0.0000042 m. Returning to the starting value confirms the conversion.

figure.purpose: Teach the reverse conversion from decimal form to a compact prefixed unit
figure.brief: Draw a reversible arrow sequence from 0.0000042 m to 4.2 x 10^-6 m to 4.2 μm. Put a small check arrow underneath that expands μ back to 10^-6. Use a different colour for number, power and unit symbol.
figure.alt_text: A reversible sequence converts 0.0000042 metres to 4.2 micrometres and checks by converting back.

blocks.title: A capital letter can change the scale by a billion
content: It can feel harmless to ignore letter case because the spoken prefix sounds clear. In unit symbols, case carries meaning.
Lower-case m means milli, or 10^-3. Capital M means mega, or 10^6. The two multipliers differ by 10^9, so 3 mA and 3 MA are not close values.
Read the prefix symbol before doing arithmetic. Also keep the Greek symbol μ distinct from m: micro is 10^-6, while milli is 10^-3.

figure.purpose: Expose the case-sensitive milli, micro and mega distinction that causes large scale errors
figure.brief: Draw three large handwritten symbol cards m, μ and M with labels 10^-3, 10^-6 and 10^6 below them. Connect m and M with a warning arrow labelled case matters, and keep the layout sparse.
figure.alt_text: Three cards distinguish milli m, micro μ and mega M by their powers of ten.

blocks.title: Mass has one special-looking base unit
content: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg. Its name already contains kilo, but kg is the base-unit symbol you must recall.
Do not stack another prefix directly onto kg. For small masses, use gram-based forms and relate them back to kilograms when needed: 1 g = 10^-3 kg and 1 mg = 10^-6 kg.
This does not change the list of five base quantities. It is a notation detail that keeps mass conversions consistent.

figure.purpose: Clarify why kilogram is the mass base unit and prevent illegal stacked-prefix notation
figure.brief: Draw a simple mass conversion strip with 1 kg, 1000 g and 1 000 000 mg shown as equal. Cross out an invented stacked-prefix form beside the strip without making it visually dominant. Use kilogram as the central labelled base unit.
figure.alt_text: A conversion strip shows one kilogram equals one thousand grams equals one million milligrams and warns against stacking prefixes on kg.

blocks.title: Name the quantity, read the scale, then compare
content: First identify the physical quantity and its SI base unit. Then read the prefix with the correct case and replace it by its power-of-ten multiplier.
Carry the unit through the arithmetic, and convert back as an independent check. Only compare measurements after they use a shared scale.

The opening timers record the same duration because 4 ms = 4 x 10^-3 s = 0.004 s. We have not rewritten any derived unit into base units or checked equation homogeneity. Those are the next two lessons.
